info.summary: The booster that lifts the whole rocket off the pad and through the thickest part of the atmosphere.
info.purpose: Provides most of the thrust for the first two and a half minutes, then separates and falls away so the rocket stops carrying its empty weight.
info.funFact: Most of a first stage's launch mass is propellant. The structure is a thin-walled can by comparison.

info.summary: Nine engines arranged in a ring around a centre engine.
info.purpose: Burns fuel and oxidizer to produce thrust. The outer engines can swivel (gimbal) to steer.
info.funFact: Clustering many small engines means the rocket can sometimes still reach orbit if one shuts down early.

info.summary: The lower tank, holding refined kerosene (RP-1).
info.purpose: Stores the fuel that the engines burn together with liquid oxygen.
info.funFact: The tanks are pressurised with helium so the walls stay stiff, a bit like a sealed can of soda.

info.summary: The upper tank, holding liquid oxygen at about −183 °C.
info.purpose: Supplies the oxygen the fuel needs to burn. There is no air to breathe in space, so the rocket carries its own.
info.funFact: The white vapour pouring off a rocket on the pad is moist air freezing against the super-cold oxygen tank.

info.summary: Small aerodynamic fins at the base of the booster.
info.purpose: Keep the rocket pointed nose-first while it is moving fast through the lower atmosphere.
info.funFact: Fins only work while there is enough air. Higher up, steering is done entirely by gimballing the engines.

info.summary: The hollow ring that joins the two stages and covers the second-stage engine.
info.purpose: Carries loads between the stages and holds the separation mechanism.
info.funFact: Separation is often done with pneumatic pushers instead of explosives, so the hardware can be reused.

info.summary: The upper stage that finishes the job of reaching orbit.
info.purpose: Takes over once the first stage is spent and accelerates the payload to orbital speed, about 7.8 km/s.
info.funFact: Reaching orbit is mostly about going sideways fast, not just going up.

info.summary: A single engine with an extra-large nozzle.
info.purpose: Provides thrust in near-vacuum, where a wide nozzle extracts more push from the exhaust.
info.funFact: This nozzle would perform badly at sea level. Air pressure would make the exhaust flow separate from the nozzle walls.

info.summary: Fuel and oxidizer tanks sharing a common wall.
info.purpose: Store propellant for the second-stage burn while keeping the stage short and light.
info.funFact: A shared tank wall saves length and mass, but it has to be well insulated because the two propellants are stored at very different temperatures.

info.summary: The rocket's flight computers, navigation sensors and radios.
info.purpose: Steers the whole vehicle, sequences events like staging, and reports telemetry to the ground.
info.funFact: Flight computers are often run in triplicate, so the rocket can vote out one that disagrees.

info.summary: Everything above the second stage: the satellite and its protective nose cone.
info.purpose: Carries the cargo the whole mission exists to deliver.
info.funFact: On many launches, the payload is only a few percent of the rocket's total mass at liftoff.

info.summary: One half of the clamshell nose cone.
info.purpose: Shields the satellite from air pressure and heating during ascent.
materials: Carbon-fibre skin over an aluminium honeycomb core
info.funFact: The fairing is dropped once the air is thin enough, because carrying it any longer is just dead weight.

info.summary: The other half of the clamshell nose cone.
info.purpose: Shields the satellite from air pressure and heating during ascent.
materials: Carbon-fibre skin over an aluminium honeycomb core

info.summary: A small communications satellite, folded up for launch.
info.purpose: Once in orbit, it unfolds its solar panels and antennas and starts its mission.
info.funFact: Satellites are shaken and blasted with loud noise on the ground to check they will survive the ride.

events.title: Countdown
events.caption: Final checks. The tanks are topped off and the flight computer takes control of the count.

events.title: Liftoff
events.caption: The engines reach full thrust and the hold-down clamps release. The rocket rises slowly at first, because it is at its heaviest.

events.title: Max-Q
events.caption: Maximum dynamic pressure: the point where speed and air density combine to put the most aerodynamic stress on the vehicle. The engines throttle down briefly to ease the load.

events.title: MECO
events.caption: Main engine cutoff. The first stage has used up its propellant and its engines shut down.

events.title: Stage separation
events.caption: The stages unlatch and push apart. Dropping the empty booster means the second stage has much less mass to accelerate.

events.title: Second-stage ignition
events.caption: The vacuum engine lights, a safe distance from the falling booster.

events.title: Fairing jettison
events.caption: The air is now thin enough that the satellite no longer needs protection, so the two fairing halves split away.

events.title: Burn to orbit
events.caption: The second stage keeps burning, now mostly accelerating sideways to build up orbital speed.

events.title: SECO: orbit
events.caption: Second engine cutoff. The payload is moving fast enough to keep falling around Earth instead of back to it: it is in orbit.
